rationale: A wins because it is tighter and makes the proof burden harder to dodge. "Going built an AI trip planner that stops short of booking" is a real distribution angle with affiliate, partner, and roadmap proof attached; B's "Mistake fares vanish fast — Going's AI wants the trip planned before they do" is a decent consumer scene, but it smuggles in urgency the update did not prove. Both sets are above the usual AI confetti pile, but B lets one extra angle stay in the room before it has earned its chair.
gaps_in_A: "now gates its first AI feature to Premium" invents "first"; the update says Going is launching an AI planner, not that it is the company's first AI feature.
"newsletter-born audiences" and "free list" import Scott's Cheap Flights history that was not supplied. Stay inside the record.
"to convert 2 million free deal-hunters" states motive as fact. Make it a conversion question unless Going says that is the strategy.
gaps_in_B: "Mistake fares vanish fast" may be true in the real world, but it is not in the supplied update. As written, the angle depends on an unstated urgency peg.
"If the prevailing push in the space is toward agents that book end-to-end" keeps a conditional trend as a kept angle. Good caveat, but it still needs outside evidence before it belongs in the set.
"end-to-end" is on the banned-word wall for a reason. Even when the meaning is clear, it smells like deck copy.
The category angle and no-booking angle overlap: "while leaving booking to links out" appears in the first angle, then comes back as "won't book your trip." Separate them harder or cut one.
